title: Transactions & ACID
description: Understand atomicity, consistency, isolation levels from read uncommitted to serializable, deadlocks, and MVCC.

segments.text: Imagine transferring money between two bank accounts. Debit one, credit the other. What if the system crashes between those two steps? Half the money vanishes. Transactions prevent this nightmare.
Atomicity means all or nothing. Either every operation in a transaction succeeds, or none of them do. If the debit succeeds but the credit fails, the entire transaction rolls back. The money is safe.
Consistency means the database moves from one valid state to another. Constraints, foreign keys, and checks are always satisfied. You can't end up with negative balances if your schema forbids them.

Isolation is the trickiest one. When two transactions run simultaneously, isolation determines how much they can see of each other's uncommitted changes. And here's where it gets interesting — there are four levels.

Read uncommitted is the Wild West. You can read data that another transaction hasn't committed yet. If they roll back, you've read data that never existed. This is called a dirty read. Almost nobody uses this level.

Read committed only lets you see committed data. No dirty reads. But you might read the same row twice and get different values if someone committed a change in between. This is called a non-repeatable read.

Repeatable read guarantees that once you read a row, it won't change during your transaction. But new rows can still appear — called phantom reads. You query 'all orders over fifty dollars,' and a new qualifying order sneaks in.

Serializable is the strictest level. Transactions behave as if they ran one after another, even though they're actually concurrent. No dirty reads, no non-repeatable reads, no phantoms. But it's the slowest because of heavy locking.
Most databases default to read committed. It's a practical middle ground — good enough consistency without too much performance overhead. Serializable is reserved for critical financial operations.
segments.thought_prompt: For an e-commerce checkout, which isolation level would you choose and why?

segments.text: When two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, neither can proceed. That's a deadlock. The database detects this and kills one transaction, rolling it back. Your application should be ready to retry.

MVCC — Multi-Version Concurrency Control — avoids many locks entirely. Instead of blocking readers, the database keeps multiple versions of each row. Readers see a consistent snapshot while writers create new versions. PostgreSQL uses this heavily.

ACID gives you safety. But every guarantee costs performance. The art is choosing the right isolation level for each operation — strict for money transfers, relaxed for analytics dashboards. Context is everything in database engineering.
segments.thought_prompt: How does MVCC help databases achieve high throughput without sacrificing isolation?
